questions.q: What does JavaScript create each time a function is called?
questions.explain: Every call gets a fresh environment. That is why two calls of createAccount produce two separate balances, and why closures made in different calls never share local variables.
options: Nothing: a function's variables are created once, when the file loads
A new environment holding that call's parameters and local variables
A copy of the whole module
A new global scope

questions.q: A function runs. Where does JavaScript look for a name that is not in the function's own call environment?
questions.explain: A function stores the environment it was created in ([[Environment]]). Its call environment links to that one, not to the caller's. This is what "lexical scope" means.
options: In the environment of the code that called the function
In the environment where the function was created, and then outwards from there
Only in the global environment
In every environment currently on the call stack, top first

questions.q: createAccount() returns { deposit, balance }, two functions created inside the same call. What is true?
questions.explain: Functions created in the same call point at the same environment. A deposit changes the variable that balance reads.
options: Each function has its own private copy of balanceKobo
Both functions share the one balanceKobo in that call's environment
balance sees the value balanceKobo had when balance was created
They share it only if balanceKobo is declared with var

questions.q: Which description of a closure is the most accurate?
questions.explain: A closure keeps a reference to its environment, not a snapshot. It sees the current value of every variable it uses, and it keeps that environment alive as long as the function itself is reachable.
options: A function that has been closed and can no longer be called
A copy of the outer variables taken when the inner function is created
A function together with the environment it was created in, which it keeps reachable and reads live
Any function declared with const

questions.q: A checkout shows a price using exchangeRate, a module variable that is updated every minute. The customer must be charged at the rate they saw. How do you lock it in a closure?
questions.explain: The factory call's parameter is a new variable that nothing assigns to again, so it keeps the value it was given. Reading the module variable would follow every later update.
options: Use exchangeRate directly inside the arrow; closures take a snapshot
Pass the current rate as an argument to a factory, quoteWithRate(exchangeRate), and use the parameter in the returned function
Declare exchangeRate with var
Call Object.freeze(exchangeRate)

questions.q: Why does for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) fns.push(() => i) give functions that return 0, 1 and 2?
questions.explain: This per-turn copy is a special rule for let declared in the for head. With var there is only one i, and all arrows read its final value.
options: Arrow functions copy the variables they use
A let in the for head gets a new environment for every turn, with the current value copied in, so each arrow captures a different i
let variables cannot change
The loop runs the arrows immediately

questions.q: This code makes every handler return the same final value of n (3). Which change fixes it? let n = 0; while (n < 3) { handlers.push(() => n); n += 1; }
questions.explain: There is only one n, declared outside the loop. A const inside the body lives in the body's block environment, which is new on every turn, and it never changes after the closure captures it. (const n would fail at n += 1.)
options: Change let n to var n
Change let n to const n
Inside the loop body, write const position = n; and capture position instead
Replace the arrow with a function expression

questions.q: Old code wraps a loop body in (function (position) { … })(i);. What problem did that solve?
questions.explain: An IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression) is a function called right where it is written. Each call creates a new environment with a new position parameter. Today let, const and array methods do the job more clearly.
options: It made the loop run faster
Before let, calling a function was the only way to get a new environment per turn, so each closure could capture its own position
It stopped the loop from running more than once
It turned the loop body into a module

questions.q: An import job creates one million order-line objects, each with the same five methods. Why might a class be better here than a closure-based factory?
questions.explain: Every call of a factory creates new functions for the returned object. With a million objects that adds up. Class methods live on the prototype and are shared by all instances, and #private fields keep data just as private.
options: Closures cannot hold numbers
Classes are the only way to keep data private
A class keeps the methods once on the prototype; a factory creates five new function objects for every order line
Classes do not use memory for their fields

questions.q: A closure-based account returns { deposit, balance }, and the methods use variables, not this. What is the practical benefit?
questions.explain: Class methods lose this when taken off their object. Closure methods find their data through their environment, so amounts.forEach(account.deposit) works.
options: The methods run faster than class methods
You can pass account.deposit as a callback on its own and it still works, because it does not depend on this
The object can be cloned with structuredClone
The methods are automatically memoized

questions.q: createFeeCalculator({ percent: 0.5, minKobo: 1000, capKobo: 200000 }) returns feeFor(amountKobo). What is this technique called, and what does it buy you?
questions.explain: Supplying some inputs now and the rest later is partial application. The closure remembers the settings, so the rest of the program never passes them around again.
options: Recursion; it avoids loops
Partial application through a factory; the settings are checked and prepared once, and callers only pass the amount
Memoization; results are cached
Hoisting; the function can be called before it is defined

questions.q: const pay = once(chargeCard). The first call is pay("ORD-7", 5000). What does pay("ORD-8", 9000) do?
questions.explain: once runs the function the first time and returns the stored result forever after, ignoring new arguments. That is right for one-time setup, and wrong as general duplicate protection for payments, which must be keyed by order id.
options: Charges ORD-8 normally
Throws an error because pay was already called
Returns the result of the ORD-7 charge again without charging anything
Charges ORD-7 a second time

questions.q: Which function is safe to memoize?
questions.explain: Memoization is only safe for pure functions: same arguments, same result, no side effects. The others read changing data or perform an action that the cache would silently skip.
options: stockOf(sku), which reads the current stock from a database
now(), which returns Date.now()
vatKobo(priceKobo), which returns Math.round(priceKobo * 0.075)
sendReceipt(email), which sends an e-mail

questions.q: A memoized totalOf(cart) uses the cart object as the Map key. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: A Map key is matched by identity, not content. Memoize functions of simple values, or build an explicit key, and never cache results for data that can change.
options: Maps cannot use objects as keys
Keys compare by identity: the same cart after it changes returns the stale total, and every new but equal cart misses the cache and adds an entry
The cart is deep-copied into the cache every time
Nothing, as long as the cart is small

questions.q: Why should a memoization cache in a long-running server have a size limit?
questions.explain: The cache lives in a closure that lives as long as the memoized function, often the whole process. Evicting the oldest entry (a Map keeps insertion order) keeps the size bounded.
options: Maps become slower to read after 100 entries
Without one, every distinct argument adds an entry forever, so memory grows until the process runs out
JavaScript deletes unbounded caches automatically
Limits make every call a cache hit

questions.q: In const result = fn(key); cache.set(key, result);, what happens to the cache when fn throws?
questions.explain: A thrown error ends the function at that line. Not caching failures is usually what you want, because the next attempt might succeed.
options: The error object is stored under the key
Nothing is stored: the throw leaves the function before cache.set runs, so the next call tries again
undefined is stored under the key
The whole cache is cleared

questions.q: Every request handler calls priceUpdates.subscribe((e) => notify(request, e)) and never unsubscribes. What happens over days of traffic?
questions.explain: The hub is long-lived and reachable, so are the listeners in it, so are the environments they closed over. Return an unsubscribe function from subscribe and call it when the work is done.
options: Nothing: listeners are removed automatically when the request ends
The hub keeps every listener, and each listener's closure keeps its request alive, so memory grows without limit
Only the most recent listener is kept
The garbage collector frees the requests but keeps the listeners

questions.q: Why call unsubscribe() inside a finally block?
questions.explain: finally always runs when the try block ends, by return or by throw. Cleanup placed there cannot be skipped by an error.
options: Because finally runs faster than normal code
So it runs whether the work returns normally or throws; otherwise every failed request would leak its listener
Because unsubscribe can only be called from finally
To stop the error from reaching the caller

questions.q: A long-lived label function is () => `${report.title}`, where report holds 50,000 rows. How do you stop it from keeping the rows alive?
questions.explain: A closure keeps alive what it uses. If it only uses a short string, the large object can be collected once nothing else refers to it (as long as no other closure from the same call still uses report).
options: Call Object.freeze(report)
Write it as a function expression instead of an arrow
Copy the title into a local const title = report.title and have the closure use only title
It is impossible; closures always keep every outer variable alive

questions.q: Why does createTransferLimit take a today function instead of calling new Date() itself?
questions.explain: Passing a dependency in makes the code testable: the limiter only needs "what day is it?", not a real clock. This is dependency injection with a function.
options: Because new Date() does not work inside closures
So tests can pass a fake clock and move to the next day instantly, while production passes one that reads the real clock
To make the limiter run faster
Because dates cannot be compared as strings

questions.q: How should you test a closure's private sentKobo variable?
questions.explain: Tests should check behaviour the same way callers see it. That also lets you change the private details later without rewriting the tests.
options: Export the variable from the module so the test can read it
Read it with limiter.sentKobo
Through the public functions: authorize some amounts, then check remainingKobo() and the results of further calls
Private state cannot be tested

questions.q: The daily limiter keeps its totals in closures. The app now runs as two server processes behind a load balancer. What breaks?
questions.explain: Memory belongs to one process. Limits that must hold across processes and restarts live in a shared store such as Redis or the database; the closure design carries over, with the store passed in like the clock.
options: Nothing: closures are shared between processes
Each process has its own totals, so a customer can send up to the limit through each process, and a restart forgets everything
The limiter throws because two copies exist
Transfers become twice as slow
Closures stop working after a restart

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: cartItems is per checkout; shopOrders is one level out, shared by both checkouts. After two Ada calls, Tunde's first call makes cart 1 and shop 3; Ada's third makes cart 3 and shop 4.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The parameter r received the value 1500 when lockRate was called, and nothing changes r afterwards. The second call receives the new rate.

questions.explain: After the first call, once returns the stored result and ignores new arguments. The wrapped function ran exactly once.
options: connected to db-1 connected to db-1 1
connected to db-1 connected to db-2 2

connected to db-1 connected to db-2 1

questions.explain: There are three distinct keys (1000, 2000, 3000). Only the first call for each runs the function; repeats are answered from the cache.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The function reads data that changes, so it is not pure. The cache answers the second call with the old value. Never memoize functions that read mutable state.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: describe was created at the top level, so its outer environment is the module's. Being called from inside report does not give it access to report's branch.
options: branch Lagos
branch Abuja
branch undefined
ReferenceError: branch is not defined

questions.q: Finish createTicketCounter(prefix, step): every call of the returned function gives the next code, counting up by step from step. Two counters must not share their count.
questions.explain: The count lives in the environment of each createTicketCounter call, next to prefix and step. The returned arrow reads and updates it.

questions.q: Write once(fn): the returned function calls fn the first time only (passing its arguments) and returns that first result on every later call.
questions.explain: Two closure variables do the work: called remembers whether fn ran, and result remembers what it returned. Both are private to this one wrapper.

questions.q: Write memoize(fn) for one-argument functions, using a Map in a closure, so that fn runs only once per distinct argument.
questions.explain: Check the cache first; on a miss, compute, store and return. The Map lives in the closure, so it survives between calls but nothing outside can touch it.

questions.q: Every handler reports the last coupon. Fix the loop so each handler reports its own coupon, keeping the while loop.
questions.explain: A const inside the loop body is a new variable on every turn, and it never changes after the handler captures it. The shared k was 3 by the time the handlers ran.
questions.expected: applied SAVE10, applied SAVE20, applied FREESHIP

questions.q: Write the factory createDiscount(percent, capKobo). It returns a function that takes a price in kobo and returns the discount: percent of the price, rounded, but never more than capKobo.
questions.explain: The settings are captured once by the returned arrow. Each discount function carries its own rate and capKobo.

questions.q: Make subscribe return an unsubscribe function that removes exactly that listener. The program subscribes two listeners, removes one, and emits.
questions.explain: The returned arrow is a closure over both listeners and the specific listener that was added, so it can remove exactly that one. Without it, subscribers can never be removed and they leak.

questions.q: Write after(n, fn): the returned function does nothing (returns undefined) for the first n - 1 calls, and calls fn from the nth call on. Use it to give a loyalty reward from a customer's third order.
questions.explain: A private calls counter in the closure counts every call. Only when it reaches n does the wrapper start passing the arguments through to fn.
questions.expected: undefined undefined reward for ORD-3 reward for ORD-4

questions.q: Finish createAccount() so the balance is private: deposit(k) adds, withdraw(k) subtracts but returns "insufficient funds" instead when k is more than the balance, and balance() reads it. There must be no balanceKobo property on the returned object.
questions.explain: The balance is a variable in the factory call's environment, reachable only by the three functions created in that call. account.balanceKobo is undefined because no such property exists.
